source: Olivier's validated daily accounts; journal-current.json and journal-day13.json through journal-day18.json. Literary transitions added without inventing events.

entries.title: The 4:30 a.m. escape
entries.summary: Nine hundred kilometres, three countries and a very peaceful first landing.
paragraphs: At about 4:30 a.m., while most of the Paris region was still asleep, we pointed Gaston north. After so much anticipation, the Lofoten Islands were finally more than an idea, a collection of maps and a suspiciously ambitious number of saved places. They were somewhere we were actually driving to.

France, Belgium, Germany: the first day belonged to the motorway. Around 900 kilometres passed beneath our rolling home, with the necessary pauses to keep the humans functioning and Paddy reasonably satisfied with the service. There was nothing glamorous about the scale of the transfer. The reward, we kept reminding ourselves, lay further north.

At roughly 6:30 p.m., we reached the Wohnmobilstellplatz im Naturschutzpark in Bispingen, in the Lüneburg Heath. After the noise and concentration of the road, the change was immediate. A quiet, pastoral corner of Germany replaced the motorway soundtrack, and we could finally stop calculating how much further there was to go that evening.

It was a simple first night, but exactly the right one. Gaston had delivered his passengers; Paddy could inspect the surroundings; we could breathe. The great northern journey had begun with a very long drive, then opened a wonderfully peaceful door.
entries.fieldNote: Departure around 04:30; arrival around 18:30. The approximately 14-hour span includes stops, not just driving.

entries.title: Two bridges to another world
entries.night: Lakeside stop in Sweden · name not recorded
entries.summary: Storebælt, Øresund, and the first Scandinavian evening by the water.
paragraphs: From Bispingen we continued north, through Denmark and towards Sweden. Another substantial day of driving lay ahead, but this time the road provided its own landmarks: the great Scandinavian bridges. Our no-ferry plan was becoming a very tangible series of enormous structures above the sea.

Storebælt and then Øresund broke the motorway rhythm. Long ribbons of road over open water made the crossing feel like a genuine threshold. We were no longer merely getting out of France. Scandinavia was here, around us, and the whole expedition suddenly acquired a different scale.

Fuel stops, pauses and more kilometres carried us into southern Sweden. The Grand North remained a long way away, but the scenery and the feeling of the journey had changed. The practical task of advancing was slowly giving way to the pleasure of being somewhere else.

That evening, the calm of a lake answered all the hours on the road. Water, nature and a quiet pitch were enough. A few stones in the landscape seemed almost deliberately arranged, like a small outdoor artwork. After two days of moving through Europe, we were learning to appreciate the rather excellent luxury of standing still.
entries.fieldNote: The exact overnight location was not preserved in the account; no campsite name or daily distance has been invented.

entries.title: Further north, a little more carefully
entries.night: Swedish lakeside campsite · name not recorded
entries.summary: A long Swedish transfer, a museum stop, and a worrying moment with Paddy.
paragraphs: We left at about seven for another long climb up the map of Sweden. Stockholm came and went, and the road continued beyond it. Sweden has a particular talent for making a serious distance look deceptively modest on a screen. Gaston, who had to do the actual work, was in a better position to judge.

A stop at Sveriges Bilmuseum, a pause near a listed heritage site and a visit to Coop punctuated the drive. These were small interruptions, but useful ones: glimpses of a country rather than just exits on a motorway. Still, the day was long — perhaps a little too long.

Then Paddy suddenly stiffened and trembled. For a few uncomfortable minutes, the itinerary lost all importance. We stopped worrying about how far north we were and concentrated on him. Rest and food helped him recover, and the relief was enormous. The episode stayed with us as a reminder of who really set the priorities on this expedition.

By evening, a lovely campsite facing a lake brought everything back into proportion. Quiet water, a gentle landscape and stones that looked like an artwork replaced the fatigue of the road. We had made progress, but the real success of the day was simpler: Paddy was himself again, and everyone could rest.
entries.fieldNote: The account records Paddy's symptoms and recovery, not a veterinary diagnosis.

entries.title: The four-hour short walk
entries.summary: Skuleskogen stole the timetable. Gaston's engine light stole the evening.
paragraphs: We set off around seven in fog thick enough to make the world feel very small. The plan was sensible on paper: roughly 500 kilometres, with a gentle walk halfway through to stretch everyone's legs, Paddy's included. A well-balanced transfer day. What could possibly go off-script?

Skuleskogen provided the answer. Our little walk became almost four hours among wooden walkways, gravel paths, rocks and lakes. Langtjärnen and Skrattabborrtjärn drew us further into the landscape, and the clock quietly ceased to matter. This was the kind of stop that justified the journey, even while it dismantled the day's schedule.

We returned to Gaston with a substantial delay and a head full of wild Swedish scenery. Then, as Umeå approached, a yellow engine warning lit up. We pulled into a Coop car park, and the day's sense of wonder gave way to a much more practical question: could we keep going?

Roadsurfer was contacted; garages were searched for; the next morning began to organise itself around an engine rather than an island. The contrast was brutal. A few hours earlier we had been happily losing ourselves in a national park. Now a small light on a dashboard appeared to hold the future of the holiday.
entries.fieldNote: The 500 km figure was that morning's target, not a measured daily distance.

entries.title: Three garages and an accidental beach
entries.night: Northbound overnight stop · name not recorded
entries.summary: A morning devoted to the EGR valve, followed by a much-needed wrong turn.
paragraphs: Day five opened with a new kind of sightseeing: garages in Umeå. The first address, around nine, was in an outlying area surrounded by wrecked vehicles. It did little to inspire confidence, and despite Sorya's efforts there was nobody available to look after Gaston. We moved on.

The second stop was friendlier and could, in principle, run a diagnostic check. Unfortunately, our vehicle was incompatible with the equipment. We paid €16 for the trouble, an amount later refunded automatically. At this point, the morning's most successful mechanical operation had been moving the camper from one unsuccessful appointment to another.

The third address was Auto Star. Sorya intercepted an employee arriving before opening, around 10:30–10:45, and at last we got an answer: an EGR-valve problem. More importantly, the garage told us we could continue. After all the uncertainty, that was the sentence we needed to hear.

Then a navigation mistake delivered a small cove and an extraordinary beach. Nothing about it had been planned, which somehow made the relief greater. We could stop, breathe and let the mechanical worries retreat for a moment. The wrong turn had excellent timing.

We resumed the journey north behind schedule, with less time than intended but the Lofoten still ahead of us. The morning had not repaired our timetable. It had restored something more useful: the possibility of carrying on.
entries.fieldNote: The €16 unsuccessful diagnostic payment was refunded; it is not an additional trip cost. The garage's assessment describes this specific incident, not general advice about warning lights.

entries.title: Somewhere near Asgard
entries.weather: Rain, with dramatic breaks in the cloud
entries.summary: After years of anticipation and a day of rain, the islands finally rose around us.
paragraphs: A big driving day, much of it in rain. We passed through Narvik and continued towards the islands, deliberately extending the stage to recover some of the time lost the day before. There was fatigue, certainly, but also the growing knowledge that we were finally close.

Then the landscape changed its language. Rock and sea, great mountain faces falling towards the water, a scale that made the road seem almost incidental. Even in the rain, the entrance to the Lofoten matched all the anticipation we had carried for three years. No screen had quite prepared us for the physical presence of those mountains.

At intervals, the rain stopped and the light broke through. The scene became almost mythological. It was easy to imagine Asgard somewhere beyond the next ridge, or a troll unfolding itself from the rock. Odin and Thor suddenly seemed less like distant names and more like entirely plausible inhabitants of this landscape.

Eventually we reached Sandsletta Camping AS. We were tired after another long stage, but this exhaustion came with something new: arrival. The Lofoten were no longer ahead of us. They were around us. Gaston could switch off, and we could finally begin the part of the journey that had pulled us all this way.
entries.fieldNote: This is the recovered 30 August story: Day 6 of the continuous 18-day chronology.

entries.title: The moose welcome committee
entries.weather: Grey but dry at Haukland; beautiful evening light
entries.summary: Wild moose, a beach café and eight kilometres of coast at exactly the right pace.
paragraphs: After the long transfer days, we finally woke with the feeling that we could take our time. The road to Haukland immediately rewarded us: a female moose and her young appeared beside it. Later came a male with antlers — the first wild bull Olivier had seen like this. Photos, videos, and that particular excitement when an animal is not part of a plan or an attraction, but simply there.

Haukland was grey, but dry. That was plenty. The beach, the water and the surrounding mountains did not need sunshine to make their point. At Haukland Beach Café, a latte and banana bread provided the correct speed for admiring it all. Olivier also found the Lofoten paragliding guide he had been looking for. Research, naturally, can involve cake.

We then walked the Haukland–Uttakleiv loop, around eight kilometres along two faces of the coast. There was time to look, stop and enjoy the landscape instead of reducing it to a quick photograph. Paddy accompanied the expedition, and the day began to resemble the trip we had hoped for.

By the time we reached Ramberg, the light was beautiful. We were tired in the good way: from walking and experiencing a place, not simply covering distance. The moose, the beaches and the coastline had made the day feel full without our having to fill every minute.
entries.fieldNote: About 8 km on foot, not 8 km driven. Gaston's troublesome step belongs to the vehicle incident log for this part of the trip.

entries.title: Breakfast takes the scenic route
entries.summary: Seasonal closures, a no-dogs café and the pleasure of finally slowing down.
paragraphs: Paddy continued his campaign against sleeping late, so we were up early again. Our first stop was Vikten, hoping for the café associated with the glassblower. The pastries and special hot drinks we had imagined were no longer being served: the season had finished before our appetite had.

At Ramberg we filled up and Olivier remembered a café with delicious breakfasts. A promising development, until we discovered dogs were not allowed. With Paddy as a full member of the party, that settled the matter. The quest for breakfast was beginning to develop its own itinerary.

We continued to Å, at the end of the road, for the traditional bakery. The pastries were perfectly serviceable rather than unforgettable, but our stomachs were grateful. The village itself was pleasant to explore, with red houses, reminders of the fishing life and that distinctive end-of-the-road atmosphere.

A coastal walk towards Yttersand softened the rest of the day. After the kilometres from France and the mechanical diversions, we were beginning to live at the islands' pace. We settled at Moskenes Camping for the night, with no major feat to report and no need for one. Finally, we were slowing down.
entries.fieldNote: The dog restriction in the account concerned the Ramberg café, not a confirmed general ban on the beach.

entries.title: The guide, the sherpa and the VIP
entries.weather: Clear skies, sunshine and ideal morning conditions
entries.summary: Nearly two thousand steps, one carried Pomeranian, and a view worth every one.
paragraphs: Some days are easy to recount. Others you would rather keep intact, somewhere safe. This was one of those days. The first achievement was getting Sorya up early — and, as it turned out, she would not regret it. Around 7:30 we reached the Steffenakken parking area near Djupfjorden, crossed the bridge on foot and made our way to Reinebringen.

The air was cool, the crowds had not arrived, and the conditions were ideal. Very quickly, our party acquired official titles: Olivier was the guide, Sorya the sherpa and Paddy the Super VIP, carried with all the appropriate honours. These roles would prove considerably more enduring than most of our original itinerary.

For Olivier, accustomed to hiking, the climb was manageable. For Sorya, not trained for that kind of effort, it was a genuine achievement: nearly two thousand steps, taken at her pace, without giving up. Add a small privileged passenger and the promotion to sherpa was thoroughly earned.

Then the world opened below us. Reine, the cut-out shapes of the fjords, mountains rising from the sea, tiny villages and extraordinarily clear light. We had travelled thousands of kilometres for moments like this, and for once there was nothing to adjust, postpone or troubleshoot. We were there, together, looking at it.

We descended without rushing and stopped in Reine for a well-earned coffee. Later, Flakstad offered a gentler walk of around an hour to an hour and twenty minutes, still under that remarkable light. By about five we were back at Moskenes. Sunshine, perfect temperatures, a clear sky and Sorya at the summit: the day had aligned itself beautifully.
entries.fieldNote: The step count is approximate. The remembered parking arrangement is part of the trip record, not current parking advice.

entries.title: The wind edits the itinerary
entries.place: Moskenes → Reine → Nusfjord → Myrland Beach → Moskenes
entries.weather: Bitter wind; a calmer programme afterwards
entries.summary: Bunes gave way to galleries, a quiet beach and Gaston's next little rebellion.
paragraphs: We woke around 7:30, a little more leisurely than the previous morning, and headed towards Reine with Vindstad and Bunes in mind. The freezing wind made the prospect of an exposed day decidedly less appealing. We abandoned the boat-and-hike idea. The weather had read the itinerary and submitted amendments.

Nusfjord became our alternative: an old fishing village to explore slowly, a pastry and something hot on the jetty, houses and harbour details to take in. The birds supplied plenty of atmosphere. It was a very different sort of day, and increasingly the right one.

The photographic and art galleries were a welcome surprise. Instead of rushing from viewpoint to viewpoint, we spent time with images, different artistic worlds and the spaces themselves. For a journey so dominated by mountains and weather, this cultural detour opened another door into the islands.

Then we looked for somewhere quieter and found Myrland Beach. Few people, room to walk, fresh air and no timetable to satisfy. Paddy got a proper outing, and we all benefited from a pause outside the busiest places.

Gaston chose the end of the day to break a door strut. We inspected the pieces and tried to understand what might need replacing; fortunately the door still closed. Back at Moskenes, the day's final inventory read: no Bunes, excellent detour, peaceful beach, one more repair to discuss. Travel has its own accounting system.
entries.fieldNote: The account confirms that we abandoned Vindstad/Bunes because of the wind; it does not independently establish whether the boat operator cancelled the sailing.

entries.title: Three hours at fjord level
entries.place: Hamnøy → kayak with Saga Adventures → Bobil Camp
entries.weather: Bright morning sunshine; headwind on the return paddle
entries.summary: An eagle, jellyfish and a return leg that our shoulders remembered.
paragraphs: It was not entirely clear whether Paddy had woken us or we had woken Paddy, but we managed to arrive in Hamnøy reasonably early, under bright sunshine. The village did not take long to explore. With red houses, mountains, water and that light, however, it made excellent use of the time.

The main event was three hours of kayaking with Saga Adventures. Our group numbered eight; Sébastien took another group of twelve. Olivier's previous experience earned him a solo kayak, and our guide Román proved both knowledgeable and genuinely pleasant company.

Román shared observations about the fjords, birds, wildlife, plants and the workings of the environment around us. From the water the islands felt different: closer, quieter, and less arranged around the road. We saw an eagle, other local birds and plenty of jellyfish.

Much of the outing was wonderfully comfortable. Then the wind changed, and the return became a more serious negotiation between paddle, water and determination. With less shelter, every stretch against the wind demanded its share of effort. By the end, Olivier's biceps and shoulder had filed a detailed report.

We continued through the islands and finished at Bobil Camp. This had been a day with fewer kilometres on foot but a completely different perspective. Three hours at the surface of a fjord had shown us a Lofoten that no roadside stop could quite provide.
entries.fieldNote: The guided outing and group sizes are recorded in the original account. No unrecorded arrangement for Paddy during the kayak session has been invented.

entries.title: One last village, then the long way home
entries.summary: Seaweed, chocolate, climbing memories and a tired arrival in Swedish Lapland.
paragraphs: We left Bobil Camp without rushing and headed for Henningsvær, curious rather than tightly scheduled. The small islands, connected streets and houses facing the sea made it a pleasure to wander. Walking there gave a sense of a village shaped first by water, then increasingly by its road connections.

For Olivier, the place also brought back a very particular memory. Four years earlier he had attempted Festvågtind carrying paragliding equipment, reaching the small lake of Heiavatnet before weight and strong conditions persuaded him to stop. Only Fab had taken off, for a magnificent flight. This visit required no ascent and considerably less equipment.

A shop selling local seaweed products, flavoured salt and chocolate supplied gifts for the family. White chocolate, dark chocolate, salt and tastes of the coast: souvenirs that would be useful long after the photographs had been sorted. Paddy, meanwhile, continued to give the walking programme his full attention.

We almost stumbled upon the famous football ground. From ground level it was less spectacular than in aerial pictures, but still wonderfully improbable on its piece of rock. Olivier also made the necessary climber's pilgrimage to Klatrebutikken beside Klatrekaféen, only to discover the trad and bouldering guides were sold out. Sorya had better luck with her fish and chips and thoroughly enjoyed them.

Then the day changed character. Hours of driving replaced the village stroll; darkness arrived and fatigue accumulated. By the time we reached Camp Alta near Kiruna, we had little capacity left to enjoy it. We simply stopped, exhausted. A lovely morning had become a demanding transfer, and the feeling was unmistakable: this time we were on the way home.
entries.fieldNote: The paragliding story is a memory from an earlier visit, not a flight made during the 2026 trip.

entries.title: Six reindeer before breakfast
entries.place: Camp Alta / Kiruna → Boviksbadet → Ove Hörnas Camping
entries.night: Ove Hörnas Camping · name as recorded
entries.summary: A freezing start, a northern farewell and thirteen and a half hours on the move.
paragraphs: At six in the morning we left Camp Alta in a temperature of −2°C. Gaston was back at work almost before the night had finished. Ahead lay a long descent through Sweden, and the practical business of reducing the distance to Stockholm and then Paris.

The North gave us one more image before letting us go. Six reindeer appeared on or immediately beside the road. In the cold early light, they slowed our departure and transformed the first kilometres into a proper moment of travel. After the Lofoten moose, this felt like another farewell committee — a less organised one, but equally memorable.

Then the road took over. Forests, wide spaces and long Swedish stretches passed for hours. It was a day devoted mainly to getting somewhere, while managing fatigue and making room for Paddy's needs. The map could suggest a clean line south; living that line was a much longer process.

Boviksbadet provided a pause by the water. After so long inside Gaston, walking and breathing outside were enough to restore some energy. No elaborate activity was required. Paddy needed his outing, and the humans needed to remember that their legs had purposes beyond sitting.

We finally reached Ove Hörnas Camping around 7:30 p.m., more than thirteen hours after leaving Camp Alta. The pitch cost 415 SEK; the fuel payment for the stage later appeared as 1,069.51 SEK. We settled with the enormous relief of having no further destination that evening.

It had been an endurance day rather than a sightseeing one, but it had begun with reindeer in the frost. The North was slipping behind us, and had still found a way to leave a strong final impression.
entries.fieldNote: 06:00–19:30 is elapsed travel time, including breaks. The 415 SEK campsite cost is in the story but not in the published expense ledger; it has not been silently added.

entries.title: Back to familiar Sweden
entries.summary: A softer forest walk, then an old paragliding spot unexpectedly next door.
paragraphs: The morning started more gently, without an alarm in the middle of the night. Even so, we were at Skuleskogen's southern entrance around 8:30. We had visited the park on the way north, but this time Stockholm lay ahead and there was no intention of letting a short walk turn into another four-hour expedition.

We gave the Swedish forest two hours. Quiet trails, wooden walkways, small bridges and Paddy trotting beside us formed a gentle transition after the scale of the Lofoten. It was less dramatic, but the familiar rhythm of the woods felt good. A buffer between the Grand North and the rest of the journey.

Then it was time to move. The contemplative morning gradually became a determined effort to reach Stockholm that evening. The kilometres added up, and around seven the city was finally there. Our new base was Bredäng Camping.

The surprise was its proximity to Sätrabadet, where Olivier had flown a paraglider four years earlier. Conditions were not suitable now, but simply being beside the place brought back part of his Swedish story. Perhaps some ground handling might be possible; in any case, this was no anonymous stop.

It was not the wildest day of the holiday. Its character was softer: returning to a country, places and memories we knew. After all the mountain scenery and road miles, Stockholm was waiting. Tomorrow would be a reunion.
entries.fieldNote: Sätrabadet flying belongs to the earlier visit. No flight or ground-handling session is confirmed for this day.

entries.title: For a few hours, home again
entries.summary: Dawn on the water, six hours on foot and three years of memories.
paragraphs: The alarm went at 4:30. Stockholm was still asleep, and Sätrabadet, just beside the campsite, offered a wonderfully quiet start. By six, Olivier was on the water in a kayak hired from Kayakomat.

Deer appeared in the early calm. Then came the encounter that would stay with him: an animal on the water, surfacing to breathe, diving, and appearing again. Not a brief shape glimpsed and lost, but a repeated presence in the first light of day. So close to a capital city, the scene felt unexpectedly wild.

Back at camp, the party regrouped: Sorya, Olivier and Paddington, bound for central Stockholm. This was not really a day of discovery. We had lived here for three years, leaving at the end of 2022. Familiar streets and views carried their own memories; walking through them felt like picking up an old conversation.

We stopped at Stora Bageriet and continued towards Djurgården. Paddy was part of the reunion too, returning to paths and smells from his own Swedish life. At Rosendals Trädgård, the gardens, greenhouses and café recalled the atmosphere we had loved: space and quiet, close to the centre yet somehow apart from it.

There were gifts to buy, places to revisit and no list of tourist sights to complete. By the end, we had walked for nearly six hours. It was a substantial day on our feet, but its weight came mostly from memory.

Back at Bredäng, we felt how different this had been from the Lofoten. The islands had given us discovery and awe. Stockholm had given us recognition. For three years this city had been home, and for a few hours it had felt that way again.
entries.fieldNote: The original spoken account calls the animal an ‘otarie’. The surfacing-and-diving encounter is preserved here without independently asserting a species.

entries.title: Drive, drive, drive — then exhale
entries.summary: A stop for the VIP, a helpful stranger and an unexpectedly luxurious Danish finish.
paragraphs: We left Stockholm at 7:30 with a programme of formidable simplicity: drive. Then drive some more. There was no summit to climb and no hidden beach at the end of a trail. The day had been assigned a clear task: make serious progress towards home, as efficiently as possible.

Fine weather softened the long descent through Sweden. The hours and landscapes passed behind Gaston's windscreen, and with them came the unmistakable feeling of turning the final pages of the northern chapter. This was a transit day, but it was still part of the journey.

Malmö offered an essential exception to the driving schedule: Arken Zoo, near IKEA, to spoil Paddy. After thousands of kilometres, beaches, trails and the privileged ascent of Reinebringen, the expedition's VIP had earned a resupply and some additional attention. His contribution to morale was, after all, considerable.

We crossed Øresund, re-entered Denmark and continued to Feddet Strand Resort. The campsite was a wonderful surprise: high-quality facilities, recently renovated washrooms in part of the site, generous surroundings and an immediate invitation to slow down. It had been named Best Campsite Denmark 2026 by ACSI, a distinction that made perfect sense to us that evening. It felt like much more than a place to sleep between two driving days.

Check-in still managed to provide one final challenge. We struggled with it just long enough for the day's fatigue to make itself known, before a truly lovely member of staff came to the rescue. Everything unlocked, and we were able to settle on an excellent pitch.

Then, at last, the engine stopped. We took Paddy for a proper walk, breathed and enjoyed the place. A day designed entirely around efficiency ended with rest, space and genuine pleasure. The journey was nearing its end, but Feddet gave us one more evening that felt like a holiday.
entries.fieldNote: The date is 9 September, Day 16 in the complete chronology. Departure time follows the more precise 07:30 account.

sources.label: Feddet's owner: Best Campsite Denmark 2026 announcement

entries.title: The Netherlands can wait
entries.night: Alfsee Ferien- und Erlebnispark, south of Bremen
entries.summary: A reluctant departure from Feddet and the sensible decision to stop short.
paragraphs: Feddet was not a campsite we wanted to leave in a hurry. After the previous day's long transfer, we lingered, enjoying its comfort and the chance to be still a little longer. A perfectly understandable decision, with the entirely predictable consequence that Gaston got back on the road later than intended.

Denmark unfolded around us, Storebælt was crossed again, and Germany returned. The goal had been to reach the Netherlands that evening, spreading the final effort more evenly before Paris. It still looked attractive as a plan. In the driver's seat, however, tiredness was gradually offering a different assessment.

Eventually, south of Bremen, we were simply too tired to continue sensibly. We stopped at Alfsee Ferien- und Erlebnispark in the Osnabrück region instead. No Dutch night after all. The most important destination now was somewhere we could stop safely.

The campsite was correct and functional. It would not compete with the most beautiful nights of the trip, and after Feddet the contrast was obvious. But it provided what mattered: a place for Gaston, a pause for us and a night's rest. Sometimes an excellent travel decision makes a rather unremarkable photograph.

Once settled, we took Paddy for a small walk. All three of us needed it. After the confinement and concentration of the road, a little fresh air and movement loosened the tension. We had no objective beyond walking together and recovering enough energy for tomorrow.

The penultimate day was not spectacular. It was practical and honest. We had left late, become tired and changed the plan accordingly. The Netherlands could wait until morning. Knowing when to stop belonged in the story just as much as knowing which mountain to climb.
entries.fieldNote: The overnight stop was in Germany, not the Netherlands. The total trip distance belongs to the following day's arrival, not this evening.

entries.title: Gaston brings everyone home
entries.place: Alfsee → Netherlands → Belgium → Paris region → home
entries.summary: Two traffic walls, nearly 8,700 kilometres and one exhausted but successful crew.
paragraphs: At five in the morning we were up. On this final day there would be no leisurely farewell to the campsite. Everything happened efficiently: Gaston prepared, Paddy back in his place, the crew moving with the determined coordination that eighteen days together had produced. Home was the only destination.

Germany presented the first wall. Heavy traffic, stressful progress and the tension of busy roads felt particularly harsh after the space of the North. The tiredness accumulated during the journey was already there, and this last stage was clearly not going to hand itself over politely.

The Netherlands brought a little respite. The road breathed more freely, and for a while so did we. Belgium followed, then the gradual approach to the Paris region. We were closer to home, but not yet beyond the hardest part.

The Parisian wall was formidable: prolonged queues, apparently endless delays and an accident nearby, occurring around the time we passed. The minutes stretched. Being so close made each remaining kilometre feel disproportionately long. We were exhausted, but attention still had to hold until the very end.

Finally, we arrived safely. Nearly 8,700 kilometres after setting out, the Paris–Lofoten–Paris loop was complete. Sorya, Paddy and Olivier were home in one piece. So was Gaston: battered by warning lights, a temperamental step, a broken strut and a stubborn fridge, but still faithful to the job. At the end of his tether, perhaps. At the end of the road, definitely.

We emptied him, bringing bags, equipment and fragments of the adventure back into the house. One last mission remained before the scheduled return the following day: cleaning, a thorough spruce-up, and dealing with or reporting the repairs he needed. That practical epilogue could wait for its turn. The driving was done.

Swedish forests, reindeer in the cold, moose beside the road, mountains rising out of the sea, Reinebringen's steps, fjord water beneath a kayak, wind, rain and unexpected kindness: all of it had travelled home with us. Paddy had been the thread running through every choice, every pause and so many of the best moments.
We were tired — properly, completely tired — and happy. Gaston could rest. Paddy could rediscover his familiar corners. The trip had ended, but the story was now ours to keep.
entries.fieldNote: Approximately 8,700 km is Olivier's reported total for the whole journey. The exact return odometer and completion of the 12 September handover are not yet recorded.
